analysis.one_liner: Bars health insurers from denying coverage or charging more for pre-existing conditions.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote: it was referred to the Senate health committee in March 2009 and died there when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have stopped health insurers from refusing to cover people because of a pre-existing illness, from imposing waiting periods before coverage starts, and from excluding those conditions from payment. It applied to employer group plans and to plans individuals buy on their own. It also required insurers to report data so the government could track what happened to premiums after the change. The bill never advanced past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of Americans with chronic conditions or past illnesses. The bill's own findings noted 45.7 million uninsured Americans in 2007 and that 44 states allowed insurers to deny coverage, limit it, or charge higher premiums because of a pre-existing condition. It also protects workers changing jobs, who under the old rules could face exclusions after even a 63-day gap in coverage.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits group health plans and group insurers from imposing any pre-existing condition exclusion or HMO affiliation period (a waiting period before coverage takes effect), under ERISA, the Public Health Service Act, and the tax code.
Requires every health insurer selling individual policies in an area to accept any eligible individual who applies and to cover them without pre-existing condition exclusions.
Extends guaranteed availability to every employer applying for coverage in a state, removing the old rules' small-employer-only limits.

Requires insurers to submit enrollee and claims data so the Secretary of Health and Human Services can monitor compliance, with civil penalties of up to $100 per covered life per day for failing to report.
Directs GAO to report on the bill's effect on affordability of coverage and on the number of uninsured and underinsured Americans.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurance companies, which would lose the ability to price or exclude people based on health status. Premiums for people already covered could have risen if costs of covering sicker enrollees spread across all policyholders, a risk the bill itself acknowledged by ordering a study of 'adverse selection' — sicker people buying insurance while healthier people stay out.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers, and premiums could rise

drawbacks.text: Guaranteed coverage without a parallel requirement that everyone carry insurance risks adverse selection: healthier people may skip insurance until they get sick, raising premiums for everyone. The bill required the Secretary to report to Congress on exactly this risk two years after enactment.

Banning health-based pricing and exclusion without an offsetting cost-control mechanism could push premiums upward for existing policyholders; the bill's own GAO-report provision asked for an accounting of its effect on affordability.
The bill addressed underwriting but not underlying medical costs, so it did not by itself make coverage affordable — only available regardless of health status.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — ending the practice of denying coverage to people with past illnesses — was large and popular: the bill cited polling showing 58 percent of Americans strongly favored requiring insurers to cover anyone who applies, even with a prior illness. The genuine cost was uncertainty about premiums, since guaranteeing coverage to sick people without making healthy people buy in could raise prices; the bill's authors acknowledged this by building in studies of adverse selection and affordability but included no individual mandate or premium subsidy to manage it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate health committee, and that is where it stayed — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — until the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Sen. Rockefeller introduced the bill on March 17, 2009, joined by Sen. Lautenberg and Sen. Brown, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
Five Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill; no further action of any kind was ever recorded on it.

The bill's findings cited 45.7 million uninsured Americans in 2007, a 60 percent four-year jump in underinsured adults, and 44 states letting insurers deny, limit, or surcharge coverage for pre-existing conditions.

The bill was one of several proposals in 2009 to guarantee coverage regardless of health status; a version of that guarantee became law in March 2010 in the Affordable Care Act, which barred pre-existing condition exclusions and took full effect in 2014. Well-informed readers know this; it is not in the provided record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers kept the ability to deny coverage, limit benefits, and charge more to people with pre-existing conditions for as long as the bill sat unactioned; the people it would have protected got nothing from this bill, gaining similar protections only later through other legislation.

for.name: Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV
for.role: U.S. Senator from West Virginia; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; the bill was referred to the HELP Committee.

for.name: Sens. Frank Lautenberg and Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at its introduction on March 17, 2009.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Edward Kennedy in 2009, succeeded by Tom Harkin)
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call record exists; the sponsor and all five cosponsors were Democrats, but the bill never got far enough to reveal how the full chamber would have split.

industries.note: The bill would have eliminated the industry's core underwriting tools in both the group and individual markets: refusing applicants, excluding pre-existing conditions from coverage, and imposing waiting periods. Insurers had built their business model around charging based on health status, and keeping that model required only that the bill never move.
The bill banned 'affiliation periods' — waiting times HMOs used before coverage became effective — removing a delay tactic that kept new members paying premiums before receiving care.
